title: Those who saw and overlooked
hook: those who saw others' faults and chose to overlook them

segments.voice: Yesterday: kamaaee, and your line: the sharers. Did you share a meal, or serve someone first? This week ran from dukh through nau nidh, help everywhere, jot, five, four, forty, and the sharers. Today, the last verb in that list. Day six hundred twenty-three.

Your roommate leaves the dishes again. A coworker takes credit for something you did. Your brother says the thing he always says at family dinners. You see it. You absolutely see it. And then there's a fork in the road, a split second where you decide what to do with what you saw. There's usually a well-worn path at that fork: we file it away, we bring it up later, we tell someone else. The Ardas, in its list of people Sikhs remember with honor, includes one group whose only deed is what they did at that fork. Today: those who saw and overlooked.
screen: `THE DISHES, AGAIN.` → `YOU SEE IT.` → `A FORK IN THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Right after those who shared their food, ran the kitchen and wielded the sword, the Ardas adds: dekh ke andith keetaa. Dekh ke: having seen. Andith: unseen. Keetaa: made it. Having seen, they made it unseen. It's a striking phrase. It doesn't say they didn't notice. They weren't naive. They saw clearly, and then they chose to treat it as if they hadn't. Sikhs hear it first about other people's faults and the wrongs done to them: they saw, and they let it go. Some also hear it about temptation: they saw what could have pulled them off course, and looked away. Gurbani has the same spirit elsewhere. Among the saloks of Sheikh Farid, the Sufi saint whose verses are in the Guru Granth Sahib, one says, in paraphrase: do good even to the one who does you harm, and don't let anger settle in your mind. Now, an important balance. The very same line of the Ardas honors those who wielded the sword. So overlooking isn't pretending injustice doesn't exist, or refusing to protect people. A Sikh is asked to stand up against cruelty. Andith is about something smaller and more daily: the slights, the irritations, the faults of the people around you that you could keep score of, and don't. A family, a friendship, a shared kitchen: each runs partly on people who quietly decided not to mention it. The Ardas puts them on the same list as the steadfast and those who wielded the sword. Their deed was invisible on purpose. That's the point.
screen: `DEKH KE: HAVING SEEN.` · `ANDITH KEETAA: THEY MADE IT UNSEEN.` · `FARID: DO GOOD TO THE ONE WHO HARMS.` · `NOT INJUSTICE: THE DAILY SLIGHTS.` · then, large: `SEE, AND OVERLOOK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one fault to overlook today. Sit and breathe. Let one small irritation come to mind, something someone does that you keep noticing. Not a real wrong that needs facing; something small. See it clearly, once. Then picture yourself setting it down, the way you'd put a pebble from your shoe back on the path. Notice the urge to pick it up again. Let it pass. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you set it down. The bell holds the time.
Andith, unseen. Dekh ke andith keetaa: having seen clearly, they chose to make it unseen.
Your line: see, and overlook. When the small fault you chose shows up today, see it, and let it go without a word. Day six hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: In every Ardas Sikhs remember those who saw others' faults and overlooked them, dekh ke andith keetaa, alongside the steadfast and those who shared, served and protected.

fork.setup: your coworker takes credit for something small you did. you see it. by dekh ke andith keetaa, what do the people in the Ardas do?
options: see it, and let it go.
fork.reveal: they saw, and made it unseen. the Ardas puts them on the same list as the steadfast and the sharers.

original.note: Gurmukhi: andith, unseen; dekh ke andith keetaa, having seen, they made it unseen.

trapdoor: what you thought: overlooking faults means being a pushover.
what it means: seeing clearly, then choosing not to keep score of the small things.
what a scholar hears: andith is the negative of dith (seen); the Ardas sets it beside tegh vaahee, so forbearance and protecting others stand together.
